title: Letter from Alfred B. Owen to the Superintendent of Immigration, p. 1
creator: Owen, Alfred B.
description: Annual report of the total of immigrants brought to Canada by Dr. Barnardo's Homes from July 1, 1900 - June 30, 1901 as 579 boys and 310 girls. The letter is typed and legibile. The letter celebrates the total and anticipates the total for the coming year will be at least 1000, and states that they have had excellent reports of the children placed thus far. It notes continued demand for children in the surrounding areas, and that they continue to restrict placements generally to farms. It describes the operation of inspections, visits, and documentation, and notes that many have used their savings to bring relatives over.

creator: Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization; Government of Canada; Lowe, John
description: Continued testimony by John Lowe, Secretary of the Department of Agriculture. title: First Report of the Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization pp. 12-13
creator: Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization; Government of Canada; Macpherson, Annie; Lowe, John
description: Conclusion of Emma G. Barber's letter, then Annie Macpherson's testimony begins and continues on page 13. Macpherson mentions that her agency had brought out 2000 children since 1870, and describes the procedures for training and caring for the children in the UK and during the journey. Macpherson details the financial arrangements, bonuses, and discounts, asserting that the special rates were declined. Macpherson outlines the supervision and visiting practices after the children were sent out, and the facilitation of communication with families in the UK, and exhibits a register of children (not included). The page ends with the note that some records were lost in a fire.

title: First Report of the Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization pp. 14-15
creator: Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization; Government of Canada; Macpherson, Annie
description: Continued testimony from Annie Macpherson, and colleagues Miss Bilbrough and Miss Barber, addresses the financials of the homes and estimates of the number of children who had been adopted. Macpherson asserts that the Homes are made available to children who return for whatever reason, but that the older boys who were succeeding well were asked to contribute money to aid in bringing other children to Canada. They discuss "black sheep" cases, but insist that many are successful. Senator Flint testifies about a home child who became an Attorney-At-Law, with assistance from his family. Flint describes attempts to train boys at various trades, which were not successful because they could make more money working for farmers.

title: First Report of the Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization pp. 22-23
creator: Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization; Government of Canada; Rye, Maria
description: Conclusion of Mr. Vail's testimony. Beginning of Maria Rye's testimony including the numbers of girls she had brought to Canada and the genesis of her project. Rye refutes assertions in the Doyle report on the grounds of factual errors and that he did not visit sufficient numbers of children or facilities. Rye states that out of the 1377 children brought to Canada, she had needed to find new placements for 290 of them, generally because of discipline problems, and that the girl whose testimony Doyle relies on was frequently moved due to "insubordination". Describes work of selecting placements and matching families.

creator: Select Committee on Immigration and Colonization; Government of Canada; Rye, Maria
description: Continued testimony of Maria Rye. Rye asserts that she does not have time for detailed record-keeping, and lacked the money to set up the kind of institutional support that Doyle recommends, and she suggests that federal funding would be needed to set up an infirmary. Rye invites a fuller investigation of the operation as a whole, and argues in favour of bringing the operation more fully under government oversight. The names of individuals who oversee placed children are listed. Rye states that there have been four deaths in the home and four out of it, of the more than 1000 children brought to Canada.
